<reason>Both sides were skilled, but A (CON) built the cleaner path to victory and closed it. A's opening mechanism point—the UNFCCC runs on consensus, not votes—was never squarely neutralized: B's own description of domination (parallel streams, staffing, 4 a.m. holdouts) is capacity asymmetry, and A's "heavier placard doesn't put Tuvaluan negotiators in six rooms" showed the remedy never touches the diagnosis. A's inclusive-threshold vs. zero-sum-ranking distinction defeated B's "we already measure it" answer, and B's honest pressure answers were converted into traps: "the queue is a feature" became the dilution dilemma (principled breadth sinks the islands the motion exists to elevate—never answered in B's closing), and the retreat from maximal weighting became the pinch (heavy enough to matter empties the room; light enough to keep emitters changes nothing). B also mischaracterized A's position as conceding "nothing can be done," which A corrected with capacity-building remedies and the loss-and-damage example. B's Rebuttal 2 was clipped for exceeding the word cap, a real execution cost. B's rhetoric and the consensus-as-steamrolling counter were genuinely strong, keeping this competitive, but A left more live, unanswered offense and supplied the decision rule: you cannot legislate the consent of the states whose actions decide the tide.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Rebuttal 2 turning B's own pressure answers into the decisive double bind: [B4.2]'s "feature, not bug" queue concession became principled-breadth-or-island-privilege dilution, and [B4.4]'s retreat from maximal weighting confirmed the pinch (weight heavy enough to block gavels empties the room; light enough to keep emitters changes nothing)—a trap B's closing never escaped.</best_rebuttal>
